newsitem.title: USA: Ryegrass spores probably not Karnal bunt - USDA.
newsitem.headline: Ryegrass spores probably not Karnal bunt - USDA.

text.p: The Karnal bunt-like spores discovered in Oregon ryegrass are probably not the Karnal bunt found in United States wheat for the first time last year, a special assistant to the Secretary of the U.S. Department of Agriculture said Wednesday.
"It will be another week or so before we know for sure... whether in fact its Karnal bunt," Paul Drazek, special assistant to Glickman, told the Wheat Quality Council's annual meeting.
"But, I think the broad consensus opinion now is that it is not Karnal bunt. Its' something different," he said.
USDA found the same spores in ryegrass from other countries "including in imports from those countries to the United States," Drazek said in a teleconferece from his Washington, D.C. office.
USDA in January began testing Karnal bunt-like spores found in Oregon ryegrass to determine if there was a link to the Karnal bunt that attacks wheat. Karnal bunt has not been found in Oregon wheat.

Drazek said wheat samples were taken from Oregon fields adjacent to ryegrass fields which did have the bunt-like spores, and the wheat tested negative for Karnal bunt. He suggested this would support arguments that the ryegrass spores could not be transfered to wheat as Karnal bunt.

The Wheat Quality Council consists of agronomists, members of the wheat industry, and government agriculture officials. The council monitors the milling quality of different wheat varieties and organizes three tours annually through major U.S. wheat production areas in the Plains and the Midwest.
